LONDON, England (CNN) -- Britain's Prince William is starting a two-month attachment with the Royal Navy on Monday, part of the future king's continued experience with various branches of the military, the Ministry of Defense said Saturday. Prince William and his father, Prince Charles, at his graduation from the Royal Air Force in April. William, 25, will spend the first part of his attachment on a basic sea safety course training in sea survival, firefighting and ship damage repair, according to the ministry. If William passes the course, as expected, he will join the HMS Iron Duke in the Caribbean, the department said. The ship's function is to support overseas British territories in the event of a hurricane and to carry out counter-narcotic operations. The prince, who will be called Sub Lieutenant Wales in the Navy, is expected to spend time aboard a frigate, a mine hunter, a submarine and helicopters during his attachment, which ends August 1, the Ministry of Defense said. William completed a four-month attachment with the Royal Air Force this year and received his pilot's wings upon graduating in April. He learned to fly three different aircraft during the attachment and is known as Flying Officer Wales within the RAF. William is also a second lieutenant in the British Army, where he serves in the Blues and Royals regiment of the Household Cavalry. The attachments are designed to provide the prince with military experience for when he becomes head of the armed forces as king. "When he becomes king, he needs to know his armed forces -- instinctively be very familiar with them -- and so he is doing this visit to the Royal Navy," said Rear Adm. Bob Cooling, the assistant chief of naval staff. William's father, Prince Charles, had a five-year career in the navy in the 1970s. Charles served on the guided missile destroyer HMS Norfolk and two frigates before qualifying as a helicopter pilot and joining a naval air squadron that operated from the aircraft carrier HMS Hermes. Prince Charles spent his last nine months in the navy in 1976 in command of the coastal minehunter HMS Bronington. William's uncle Prince Andrew served 22 years in the Royal Navy as a helicopter pilot, seeing active service during the Falklands War between Britain and Argentina in 1982. Queen Elizabeth II's husband, Prince Philip, William's grandfather, spent more than 13 years in the Royal Navy. He saw active service throughout World War II and was in Tokyo Harbor when Japan surrendered.

**Headline: From Flight Suits to Sailor Blues: Why Prince William is Heading to Sea**

**LONDON —** Second-in-line to the throne, Prince William, is setting sail today on a new chapter of his military career. Following a stint in the Army with the Household Cavalry and a recent attachment with the Royal Air Force—where he proudly earned his wings—the 25-year-old prince is embarking on a five-week attachment with the Royal Navy. 

Known in the senior service as Sub-Lieutenant Wales, the Prince will spend time at the Britannia Royal Naval College in Dartmouth before joining the crew of the Type 23 frigate HMS *Iron Duke* for a deployment to the Caribbean. 

To the casual observer, William’s rapid rotation through Britain’s armed forces might look like a royal game of musical chairs. However, Palace officials stress that this attachment serves a vital, long-term purpose: preparing a future King for his ultimate constitutional role as Commander-in-Chief of the British Armed Forces. 

By experiencing life in the Army, the RAF, and now the Navy, Prince William is completing what St James’s Palace calls a "tri-service attachment." During his time aboard HMS *Iron Duke*, William won't merely be observing from the bridge; he is scheduled to take part in active operations, including anti-narcotics patrols and potential hurricane relief efforts in the West Indies. 

Yet, as Prince William steps aboard ship, he does so under the long shadow of royal naval history. How does the young prince’s condensed, fast-track naval training compare to the maritime careers of his grandfather, father, and uncle?

### **The Grandfather: Prince Philip’s Wartime Valor**
When comparing royal naval service, the benchmark remains the Duke of Edinburgh. Unlike his grandson, Prince Philip was not taking a "taster course." Joining the Royal Navy as a cadet in 1939, Philip saw real, bloody combat during the Second World War. He was mentioned in despatches for his bravery during the Battle of Cape Matapan in 1941 and was second-in-command of the destroyer HMS *Wallace* at the age of just 21. 

Prince Philip was a true career naval officer whose rising trajectory was only cut short by the unexpected death of King George VI and his wife’s accession to the throne. For Philip, the Navy was a primary vocation; for William, it is one facet of a broader royal apprenticeship.

### **The Father: Prince Charles and Command at Sea**
Prince Charles followed his father’s footsteps into the Navy in the 1970s, but his service was far more extensive than William's current posting. After attending Dartmouth, Charles served on the guided-missile destroyer HMS *Norfolk* and several frigates over a five-year naval career. 

Crucially, Prince Charles achieved what few royals do: actual command. In 1976, he spent his final ten months in the Navy commanding the coastal minehunter HMS *Bronington*. While Prince William will gain valuable operational experience on HMS *Iron Duke*, his brief attachment means he will never shoulder the ultimate, lonely responsibility of commanding a Royal Navy warship as his father did.

### **The Uncle: Prince Andrew’s Combat Service**
Perhaps the most direct contemporary comparison is Prince Andrew. The Duke of York was a career officer who served in the Royal Navy for over 20 years. Most famously, as a 22-year-old helicopter pilot aboard HMS *Invincible*, Andrew flew operational missions during the 1982 Falklands War, acting as a decoy to draw Exocet missiles away from British ships. 

Andrew’s service was defined by active combat exposure and decades of routine military duty. William, by contrast, is restricted by modern security concerns and his status as a future Monarch, which limits his ability to be deployed in high-risk combat zones long-term.

### **A Modern Prince for a Modern Military**
Why the difference in approach for the young prince? Times have changed, and so has the role of the Heir. 

In the mid-20th century, a prince could dedicate five to twenty years purely to the military. Today, Prince William must balance his service with an increasingly demanding schedule of royal duties, charity work, and public engagements. Furthermore, modern military doctrine emphasizes joint operations, making William’s "tri-service" overview far more relevant for a 21st-century sovereign than specializing in just one branch.

While Sub-Lieutenant Wales will not match the deep-sea credentials of his grandfather, the command experience of his father, or the combat record of his uncle, his upcoming weeks on HMS *Iron Duke* offer something equally valuable: a genuine taste of life below deck, hard physical work, and the reality of modern naval operations. 

As he prepares to haul lines and stand watch in the Caribbean heat, Prince William is proving that while his path to the throne is unique, he is determined to earn the respect of the men and women he will one day theoretically command.

**LONDON** — Prince William is set to take to the high seas for the final leg of his intensive tri-service military training, stepping into a well-trodden Royal tradition as he prepares to join the Royal Navy for a five-week attachment. 

Sailing under the military title of Sub-Lieutenant William Wales, the 25-year-old future king will board the Type 23 frigate HMS *Iron Duke* in the Caribbean. The deployment will subject the prince to the full rigors of naval life, ranging from high-stakes anti-narcotics operations to potential hurricane relief efforts in the region.

The attachment marks the culmination of a tailored military familiarization program designed to give the prince a comprehensive understanding of the British Armed Forces—a crucial foundation for a man who will one day serve as Commander-in-Chief of the nation's military forces.

---

### A High-Stakes Deployment at Sea

During his time aboard HMS *Iron Duke*, Sub-Lieutenant Wales will not receive royal treatment. Naval officials have stressed that William will be fully integrated into the ship's 185-strong crew, sharing cramped quarters and taking on standard operational rotations.

His duties will include serving as an Officer of the Watch, navigating the vessel, participating in boarding parties aimed at interdicting drug smugglers in the West Indies, and training in maritime disaster relief operations. He is also expected to spend time with the ship’s Lynx helicopter flight crew, building on his recent aviation experience.

"Sub-Lieutenant Wales will be treated no differently than any other young officer on board," said Rear Admiral Sir Richard Ibbotson, Deputy Commander-in-Chief Fleet. "He will experience the harsh realities, the fatigue, and the immense camaraderie of life at sea. The Royal Navy operates on teamwork, and William will be an essential cog in that machine during his deployment."

Commander Mark Essig, Commanding Officer of HMS *Iron Duke*, expressed enthusiasm for the prince’s arrival: "The ship’s company is immensely proud to welcome Sub-Lieutenant Wales aboard. We have a demanding deployment ahead in the Caribbean, and he will be thrown straight into the deep end—from bridge operations to boarding routine drills."

---

### Completing the Tri-Service Puzzle: Army and RAF Background

The naval deployment completes a broad sweep across all three branches of the British Armed Forces for Prince William.

His military journey began in earnest at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, where he was commissioned as a second lieutenant into the Blues and Royals (Household Cavalry) in December 2006. As a troop commander, William trained to lead armored reconnaissance units. However, like his younger brother Prince Harry, his desire to serve on the frontlines in Iraq was ultimately stymied by senior commanders due to the unacceptable security risks posed to him and his men. 

Recognizing his long-term strategic role, the Ministry of Defence designed a customized path across the other services. Earlier this year, William completed a four-month attachment with the Royal Air Force (RAF). Stationed at RAF Cranwell, he successfully earned his RAF wings—presented to him by his father, the Prince of Wales—after learning to fly the Tutor basic trainer, the Tucano, and the Squirrel helicopter. During his RAF stint, he also gained operational experience flying C-17 Globemaster transport aircraft and the RAF’s flagship Typhoon fast jet.

Speaking on William’s progression, Air Chief Marshal Sir Glenn Torpy noted: "Prince William demonstrated exceptional aptitude during his time with the Royal Air Force. His achievement in earning his wings was hard-won, reflecting the same standards required of any RAF pilot."

---

### A Maritime Dynasty: Father, Uncle, and Grandfather

By joining the Royal Navy, Prince William aligns himself with a deeply rooted family tradition. The Royal Family's ties to the senior service are among its most historic and profound, heavily shaping the lives of William’s immediate predecessors.

#### **His Grandfather: Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh**
Prince Philip enjoyed a distinguished, hero's career in the Royal Navy during the Second World War. Entering the Royal Naval College, Dartmouth, in 1939 as a top cadet, Philip served aboard HMS *Valiant* during the Battle of Cape Matapan in 1941, where he was mentioned in despatches for his skill operating the searchlights during a chaotic night engagement. By age 21, he had become one of the youngest first lieutenants in the Navy while serving on HMS *Wallace*. His active military career was only cut short by the accession of Queen Elizabeth II in 1952, though he eventually achieved the rank of Admiral of the Fleet.

#### **His Father: Prince Charles, Prince of Wales**
Prince Charles followed his father’s footsteps into Dartmouth, serving in the Royal Navy between 1971 and 1976. After qualifying as a helicopter pilot, Charles served aboard the guided-missile destroyer HMS *Norfolk* and the frigates HMS *Minerva* and HMS *Jupiter*. In 1976, he took command of his own ship, the coastal minehunter HMS *Bronington*, for his final ten months of active service—a command he often remembers as one of the most rewarding periods of his life.

#### **His Uncle: Prince Andrew, Duke of York**
Perhaps the most dramatic modern naval service was that of Prince Andrew. A career officer, Andrew joined the Royal Navy in 1979 as a helicopter pilot. When the Falklands War broke out in 1982, he deployed aboard the aircraft carrier HMS *Invincible*. Flying Sea King helicopters, Prince Andrew flew dangerous, anti-submarine and surface search missions, and famously acted as a decoy pilot to draw Exocet missiles away from British shipping. He remained in the Navy for 22 years, eventually retiring with the rank of Commander.

---

### Looking Ahead

For Prince William, the upcoming weeks aboard HMS *Iron Duke* represent more than just a military requirement; they represent a rite of passage for a future monarch. 

Following his time at sea, the prince is expected to spend time working with the Ministry of Defence and spending time on attachments with various government departments to prepare for his eventual role as head of state. 

However, for the next five weeks, Royal protocol will give way to naval discipline. As one senior officer at Navy Command noted, "At sea, salt spray doesn't distinguish between royalty and a junior officer. Sub-Lieutenant Wales is about to find that out firsthand."
